questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 & -3 \\ -2 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 & 0 \\ -4 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the nonsingular matrix $P$ and the block diagonal matrix $B$ shown above, where the $2\times 2$ block of $B$ is a rotation-scaling matrix.
Given that $A=PB{P}^{-1},$ what are the complex (not real) eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenvectors of $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $A$ is a $3\times 3$ real matrix that has one real eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}$ with corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1},$ and two complex eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{3}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{3},$ then $A=PB{P}^{-1},$ where

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \text{Re}({\lambda }_{2}) & \text{Im}({\lambda }_{2}) \\ 0 & -\text{Im}({\lambda }_{2}) & \text{Re}({\lambda }_{2})\end{aligned}],\,\,P=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {v}_{1} & \text{Re}({v}_{2}) & \text{Im}({v}_{2}) \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that swapping the blocks on the main diagonal of $B$ will result in switching the corresponding columns in $P.$

- From our block diagonal matrix 

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 & 0 \\ -4 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

we deduce the complex eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1,2}=3\pm 4\text{i}$ and the real eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$

- From our matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 & -3 \\ -2 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

we deduce that the complex and real eigenvectors are

$$
{v}_{1,2}=[\begin{aligned}5\pm 4\text{i} \\ -2\pm 3\text{i} \\ \pm \text{i}\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 9 \\ 5 & 6 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ shown above. Find a block diagonal matrix $B,$ where the $2\times 2$ block represents a rotation-scaling matrix, such that $A=PB{P}^{-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $A$ is a real $3\times 3$ matrix that has one real eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}$ with corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1},$ and two complex eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{3}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{3},$ then $A=PB{P}^{-1},$ where

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \text{Re}({\lambda }_{2}) & \text{Im}({\lambda }_{2}) \\ 0 & -\text{Im}({\lambda }_{2}) & \text{Re}({\lambda }_{2})\end{aligned}],\,\,P=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {v}_{1} & \text{Re}({v}_{2}) & \text{Im}({v}_{2}) \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Swapping the blocks on the main diagonal of $B$ will result in switching the corresponding columns in $P.$

To compute the eigenvalues of $A,$ we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & 9 \\ 5 & 6-\lambda  & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (6-\lambda )((-1-\lambda )^{2}-9(-1)) & =0 \\ (6-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +10) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the real eigenvalue is 
${\lambda }_{1}=6.$
Now, using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{2,3} & =\frac{-2\pm \sqrt{(2)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 10}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-2\pm \sqrt{-36}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-2\pm 6\text{i}}{2} \\  & =-1\pm 3\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the block diagonal matrix is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071697/assets/5fd08491c00587e0efa4017850407c58af8ad0821c2c1aab512ec20b5295d128.png)
The vectors $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_3$ are the eigenvectors of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues $\lambda_1=7 + 4\textrm{i}$ and $\lambda_3=-3 + 2\textrm{i},$ respectively. 
Given that $A=PBP^{-1},$ find a possible matrix $P.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $A$ is a $4\times 4$ real matrix that has complex eigenvalues 

$\qquad$ ${\color{red}\lambda_1}=\overline{\color{red}\lambda}_{\color{red}2} \quad$ and $\quad {\color{blue}\lambda_3}=\overline{\color{blue}\lambda}_{\color{blue}4}$ 

with corresponding eigenvectors 

$\qquad$ ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} = \overline{\color{red}\mathbf{v}}_{\color{red}2} \quad$ and $\quad {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_3} = \overline{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}_{\color{blue}4},$ 

then $A=PBP^{-1},$ where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071697/assets/c8b3063b226f25c53f064e3f427446da7cc4c7cd99a20b8c1d9e46d33bd429e0.png)
and
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071697/assets/0489fb7ddf3f73682e4e61345fa73a601c5f8ae01bf319918becd9c2426cc73d.png)
Swapping the blocks on the main diagonal of $B$ will result in switching the corresponding columns in $P.$

From our block diagonal matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071697/assets/350a5319ff61e3f794e780561616c7a9523f18832ee040ce8faa0825818f8f24.png)
we deduce that the first and second columns of $P$ will correspond to the complex eigenvector ${\color{red}{\mathbf{v}_1}},$ and the third and forth columns of $P$ will correspond to the complex eigenvector ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_3}.$ Therefore,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071697/assets/c6213ccfec2acbc449e38e431ef1d60d2e06b19066b735faa6426dfd4b326c9c.png)
